name: PT Petrindo Jaya Kreasi Tbk

frontmatter.title: CUAN: a Barito-group acquisition vehicle re-underwritten on the book of its parts
frontmatter.summary: Revision, konglo lens. The largest part, the Petrosea stake, is now marked at PTRO's book equity, not at its market premium: a konglo sibling that is uncovered must not enter the parent's fundamental at market. The parts give a fundamental value of Rp46 a share, the price is Rp505, and the lens keeps part of the premium, for a SELL target of Rp323 — total return -36.1%.
thesis: CUAN is a listed vehicle of the Barito group, and this revision reads it as one. The largest part is a stake in the listed contractor Petrosea, and because Petrosea is itself a konglo name that is not yet covered, the group-consistency rule forbids marking it at market: the stake is carried at its share of PTRO's reported book equity, and the listed premium is excluded from the fundamental value.

The parts, at book, are worth far less than the price. The sum of the parts returns Rp39 a share and the P/BV cross-check Rp47; the twelve-month fundamental value is Rp46 against a price of Rp505, so the market pays 12.5 times today's fundamental value. The konglo lens then keeps part of that gap for twelve months, and the probability-weighted target is Rp323.

The largest mark is no longer a market mark, and that is the point. Petrosea is capitalised at US$2,182.1m of market value on US$321.4m of its own reported equity; that premium is disclosed but excluded, and the base carries the stake at US$321.4m times our 46.7%. A reader who thinks the book itself is optimistic should read the parts as a ceiling, not a floor.
The parent has partly supported that asset itself: its own subsidiary, Kreasi Jasa Persada, bought PTRO shares with the group's capital through 2025. We carry that as a bear point, not a footnote.

Earnings quality remains the hidden problem: audited operating profit is dominated by non-cash investment gains, the last audited year used cash in operations, and the finance cost consumes most of the margin the coal ramp has restored. The SINI acquisition and the power project carry no value we can source, and we say so rather than invent one.

catalysts.event: OJK hands over, in person, the administrative sanction letters from the enforcement round that includes CUAN
Petrosea extraordinary general meeting for the approval of its rights issue, which dilutes the group's listed stake if not taken up
RKAB production-quota approval for FY2027, the supply-discipline lever that governs the group's tonnage plan
FY2026 audited accounts due, the first full year in which the coal ramp and the new offshore EPCI line are both in the base
MSCI's deadline for a decision on reclassifying Indonesia to Standalone Market status, the index event that governs the regime for concentrated-ownership names

blocks.text: **This revision changes the target because the largest part is no longer marked at market.** In the last edition the Petrosea stake was carried at PTRO's traded market capitalisation, which is the single reason the target sat as high as it did. That mark broke the konglo method card's group-consistency rule: PTRO is a group sibling that is not yet covered, so its own premium must not enter CUAN's fundamental value. The Director ruled on 28 October 2026 that the stage machine cannot return this name to draft, so the stake is now carried at its share of PTRO's reported book equity and the market mark is disclosed but excluded [S3, S11]. The fundamental value is Rp46 a share and the price is Rp505, so the market pays 12.5 times today's fundamental value of Rp40; the base regime case closes 35% of the log gap over the year and the probability-weighted target is Rp323 — **SELL, target Rp323 against a price of Rp505, a total return of -36.1%** [S0]. The rating survives; the target does not, which is what the red team said it would find.

**What the sum of the parts says on book marks.** The primary method, weighted 83% of the blend, returns Rp39 a share. It has five components. The first is the group's holding in Petrosea: 46.7% of PTRO at its reported total equity of US$321.4m at the half-year date, a book mark [S3]. The second is the group's own coal concessions, carried at the reported invested capital in the mines of US$381.9m [S3], against the company's stated reserves of 228 Mt [S7]. The third is the mineral and power projects, at the reported exploration and evaluation value of US$44.3m [S3]. The fourth is the FVTPL portfolio, US$228.8m of quoted equity in non-financial institutions, carried as a financial asset at fair value rather than netted against debt as cash [S3]. The fifth is the group's other net assets, carried at book so the parts reconcile to the parent's reported equity; without it the gross marks omit the working capital and understate the group [S0, S3]. Against those we charge holdco net debt on a cash-only basis and the holding-company discount [S0]. The P/BV cross-check returns Rp47, 21.8% versus the primary [S0].

**What moves the value.** The mark on Petrosea is still the largest single line, but it is now a book mark that moves only with Petrosea's reported equity and with a coverage house value, not with the tape. The second lever is the discount, held at 30% and the only channel the scenario layer has into a static mark. The third is the financing: a discount rate of 10.7% charged on the whole against an EBITDA the half year only just covers [S3, S0]. The largest upside is a published PTRO house value above book; the largest downside is an impairment of the book itself.

PT Petrindo Jaya Kreasi Tbk (CUAN) is an energy and resources group assembled by acquisition inside the Barito group. On the annual report's own register at the end of 2025, Prajogo Pangestu holds 84.1% directly and the public holds 15.9%, across tens of thousands of holders [S2]. The valuation's insider and float figures (82.2% and 18.6%) are the data pack's snapshot, not the annual report's register; section six reconciles them, and the register is the primary figure [S2, S0]. The structure is a holding one in substance: the parent holds operating subsidiaries directly and a listed company through a wholly owned vehicle, and the single most valuable entry on this note's balance sheet is that listed stake [S3].

The group reports three segments. Mining covers both the group's own coal sales and the mining contracting it performs for others; engineering and construction and the offshore EPCI line are the contracting businesses; services is the logistics and port arm [S3]. The revenue note splits the half-year total of US$736.1m into coal sales of US$249.3m, mining services, construction and engineering, services and the new offshore oil-and-gas EPCI line, in roughly equal thirds between coal and the contracting complex [S3]. That split matters: the cash the group earns from its own concessions is a minority of consolidated revenue, and the contracting lines are pass-through work with a thin margin and concentrated counterparties [S3].

The listed subsidiary is Petrosea, in which the group holds 46.7% and which it consolidates on the basis of a control statement given by another shareholder, CRO, which holds 34.0% and provided the statement on 7 November 2023 [S3]. That is a thin control basis worth stating plainly: the consolidation rests on a third party's letter, not on an outright majority, and section five carries it as a governance risk. Petrosea brings the mining contracting, the engineering and construction business, the new offshore EPCI line, and — through the Hafar, HBS and Scan-Bilt acquisitions — contracting in Papua New Guinea [S2, S3]. It earned US$543.5m of revenue and US$1.3m of continuing net profit in the half year, on equity of US$321.4m — to which the same note adds a discontinued-operation profit of US$7.6m that the interim filing labels but does not name, sitting in the mining segment and already inside Petrosea's traded price [S3].

The group's own coal business runs through named subsidiaries with disclosed licences and lives: Multi Tambangjaya Utama holds a generation-three coal contract of work with the longest tenure, alongside Tamtama Perkasa, Borneo Bangun Banua, Intan Bumi Persada, Cristian Eka Pratama and the two development concessions [S2, S7]. Gold and silver sit in Intam, silica sand in Silika Salut Jaya, and the power project in the Guna Darma Integra vehicle [S7]. The growth strategy is acquisition-led: the company has begun negotiations to acquire control of PT Singaraja Putra, which has not closed [S2].

The footprint is domestic — Central and East Kalimantan — with the Papua New Guinea and offshore arms coming through the listed subsidiary [S2]. Competitively the group is a challenger in coal, and its integration — hauling, barging, port and contracting — is a real cost advantage; the related-party web that funds it is the channel the earnings-quality card tells us to scrutinise [S2, S3].

The industry frame for this name is a conglomerate frame, not a coal frame, and that is the change this update keeps. The group's cash generation is driven by thermal and metallurgical coal, which is supply-disciplined and policy-rationed in Indonesia: production is gated by the annual RKAB work plan and budget, and the domestic market obligation requires producers to sell a share of output into a capped domestic power market [S2, S7]. The company names compliance with the domestic obligation as a risk in its own annual report, and states the royalty rate it pays on open-pit coal at or above 5,200 kcal/kg as 13.5% [S2, F14].

The macro desk's regime is balance-of-payments pressure, neutral on thermal coal and averse on the rate-sensitive, current-account-levered domestic complex [S0]. That matters twice: the group is a leveraged domestic vehicle with a dollar-reporting balance sheet and rupiah-denominated debt, so the exchange rate of Rp18,350/USD is a live translation risk on debt serviced from dollar cash flow [S0, S3]; and the coal price is the driver our own deck carries, so the deck's path — not the company's ambition — is the revenue ceiling [S0]. The SOTP is deliberately deck-independent: the marks are book values, and the coal deck prices the operating cross-check, not the parts. No deck driver is wired into the target, and this paragraph says so rather than implying a link the model does not have.

The relevant peer set is the conglomerate group on this desk, not the coal producers: a thermal producer is valued on reserve life and cash margin, a holding company on the market marks of what it holds less its own costs and debt, then discounted [S0]. Market structure is unfavourable to pricing power — mining contracting is competitive, the group is a mid-tier coal producer with no first-quartile cost claim, and the buyers are concentrated [S3]. The moat, such as it is, is the licence base and the logistics corridor, marked in section four at the invested capital the group carries [S7, S3].

Consolidated revenue reached US$1,215.6m in FY2025 on coal sales of US$423.4m and the contracting book, and the half year to June 2026 ran at US$736.1m, up by roughly three-fifths on the comparable half of the prior year [S2, S3]. Our forecast holds the half-year's revenue run rate into the full year and tapers thereafter, and the margin structure at the half-year's own level: gross margin of 13.8%, an opex charge of 5.7% of revenue and depreciation, depletion and amortisation of 12.7% [S3]. That gives an EBITDA margin of roughly a fifth and an operating line that finally clears the interest charge, unlike the last audited year [S3].

The last audited year is the reason this note opens with the earnings-quality card. FY2025's reported operating profit was US$239.1m, of which US$193.7m was other operating income that the company describes as investment gains on other financial assets — non-cash, and most of the total [S2]. Strip it out and the group's audited operating profit was a fraction of its gross profit of US$160.0m; the engine's EBIT line, excluding that income, is US$25.3m [S2, S0]. The cash-flow statement tells the same story from the other side: after interest and tax payments the group used US$-27.6m of cash in operating activities in FY2025, a year for which it reported net profit of US$152.0m [S2]. The half year is better but not clean: operating cash flow before interest and tax was positive, and after finance costs and tax it was still a use of cash, while finance expenses of US$57.5m ran against gross profit of US$101.6m [S3].

Restating the data pack from the filing remains part of this update. The pack's depreciation is a small fraction of the audited charge, its dividend paid is several times the distribution the accounts show, and its interest expense is below the filing's finance line [S0, S2]. Each is an optics-class item, disclosed rather than concealed, not a manipulation-class flag [S2]. The depreciation restatement now runs history and forecast on one footing: the last audited year's charge is the full group figure of US$155.3m from the operating-segment note, not the cost-of-revenue depreciation component alone, so the audited year's clean EBITDA of US$180.6m and the forecast D&A rate are measured the same way and the year-on-year margin comparison is not distorted by a change of base [S2].

The balance sheet is where the holding-company frame bites. At the FY2025 balance-sheet date the group carried interest-bearing debt of US$1,448.7m [S0]; at the half-year date the filing shows short-term bank loans of US$63.2m inside a debt stack that also runs to long-term bank lines, bonds and sukuk, against cash of US$220.2m and further financial assets of US$228.8m [S3]. The data pack strikes the half-year debt at its own total [S0], and our model rolls the cash forward to US$349.3m by the end of FY2026E — a forecast, not an actual. Parent equity was US$347.2m and the total non-controlling interest US$291.2m, of which US$271.0m sits in the listed subsidiary and the rest in the two smaller non-wholly-owned subsidiaries [S3]. Capital spending ran at US$72.9m in the half year, funded by the shelf bond and sukuk programme — US$178.8m of target proceeds across two phases — and by bank facilities in which the listed subsidiary and the parent are joint borrowers [S3]. The dividend is a token: US$2.0m, or US$0.0002 a share [S2].

**Why this method set fits.** The group's most valuable asset is a holding in another listed company, and no single-product cash-flow model can carry that: a coal template would either ignore the holding or double-count the contracting revenue that flows through it [S3]. A sum of the parts treats each claim separately. The cost of capital is built on the dollar risk-free rate of 5.0%, the industry unlevered beta of 0.90 re-levered to the group's debt-to-equity of 0.45 to give 1.22, and a mature-market equity risk premium plus a country premium, for a cost of equity of 13.1% and a weighted average cost of capital of 10.7% [S0].

**The basis: the Petrosea stake at book, not at market.** PTRO is konglo:true and uncovered: its queue item is an initiation still pending, and its folder holds only a data pack. The konglo method card's group-consistency rule is explicit that a konglo sibling which is not yet covered must not be marked at market, because its own premium would enter the parent's fundamental value and the lens would then multiply it. The Director ruled on 28 October 2026 that, since the stage machine cannot return this ticker to draft, the SOTP must carry the 46.7% stake on a sourced non-market basis and disclose a below-market sensitivity. We therefore carry it at PTRO's reported total equity of US$321.4m at 30 June 2026 times our stake — the book value attributable to the stake, labelled method book [S3]. PTRO's market capitalisation of US$2,182.1m at the 15 October 2026 price is disclosed here and in section five but is NOT in the target. When PTRO publishes, this mark switches to PTRO's house value, and the increment over book — positive or negative — enters the parent; until then the listed premium is excluded by the group-consistency rule. The house has already held another konglo parent in draft for the identical reason; this name cannot be returned to draft, so the compliant book mark is the substitute [S0].

**The sum of the parts, line by line.** The primary method is weighted 83% of the blend. Its first component is the Petrosea stake at book, as above [S3]. The second is the group's own coal concessions, carried at the group's reported invested capital in the mines — mining properties and stripping activity assets of US$381.9m at the half-year date [S3] — against the company's stated reserves of 228 Mt [S7]. Those mining properties are the group's own concession areas of interest, the Tamtama Perkasa and MUTU holdings; the group's mining permits and contract of work are held by the coal subsidiaries, not by the listed contract-mining subsidiary, so the block is not double-counted against the Petrosea mark [S3, F85]. We carry it at book rather than on a multiple for a stated reason: the company prints no segment EBITDA, and its only printed EBITDA figure is dominated by non-cash investment gains, so a multiple of it would import the earnings-quality problem [S4, S2]. A value per reserve tonne would need a transaction or peer benchmark the archives do not carry: we searched [S2], [S3] and [S7] and found none, so the block stays at book, and the bull case carries the production ambition [S4/F13] and the coking-coal start [S6] as qualitative upside the static-mark scenario layer cannot itself price. The third component is the projects, at the reported exploration and evaluation carrying value of US$44.3m, the floor the most-likely card requires for development assets rather than an estimate of their worth [S3]. One item we do not add as a sixth component, and say so: the equity-method investment in associates of US$34.0m is not marked separately, because its material financial-services leg is held through the listed subsidiary's own subsidiary and so already sits inside the Petrosea mark, and the residual is immaterial against the parts [S3, F86].

**The FVTPL portfolio and the net-debt arithmetic.** The fourth component is the portfolio of US$228.8m of other financial assets. Note six says these are investments in non-financial institutions, classified as financial assets at fair value through profit or loss and measured at quoted bid prices in an active market — equity securities, realisable but not demand deposits [S3]. We therefore carry them as an asset at fair value and do NOT net them against debt as cash, which is the change this revision makes: the last edition treated the pack's cash figure, which is cash of US$220.2m plus this portfolio, as if both were cash. On a cash-only basis the holdco charge is group interest-bearing debt, less cash of US$220.2m, less Petrosea's debt taken by entity — its share of the syndicated facilities of US$161.9m, its own bonds of US$53.4m plus US$56.0m, and its own sukuk ijarah of US$26.2m plus US$28.0m [S3]. Petrosea's debt is excluded because the stake is marked at equity, which is already net of it; the parent's own bond and sukuk programmes (US$112.0m of bonds and US$19.6m plus US$36.4m of sukuk wakalah) and the entity-unattributed bank lines stay in the charge, the latter the conservative direction for a SELL [S3]. The resulting holdco net-debt charge is larger than the last edition's by the US$228.8m portfolio, which is now an asset rather than a netted cash item; the charge is stated in full in the model schedule, and the arithmetic above is the whole of it.

**The fifth component, and why it is there.** The group's remaining net assets — operating working capital, restricted funds, other receivables and property other than the mining properties and exploration assets — are carried at book as a single row. Without them the gross marks would omit the working capital and other net assets and understate the group against its own audited equity, so the row is the residual that makes the parts reconcile to parent equity of US$347.2m, not a new mark [S3]. At all-book marks a sum of the parts equals book equity; that identity is the check on this construction.

**Look-through leverage.** The sentence to correct is the last edition's claim that the subsidiary's borrowings sit inside the consolidated debt we deduct: they do not, because the SOTP deliberately excludes Petrosea's debt by entity and marks the stake at equity. The two debt stocks are kept separate. The holdco charge above is struck after removing Petrosea's debt; adding back the group's 46.7% share of Petrosea's US$161.9m, US$53.4m plus US$56.0m and US$26.2m plus US$28.0m gives the look-through debt base, which we measure against clean EBITDA of US$180.6m — EBIT of 25.3 plus the full D&A of US$155.3m [S2, S3]. Even at book the leverage is high, and it is the reason the equity has little room to absorb a de-rating of the marks.

**Holdco overhead: disclosed, not invented.** The card asks for parent-level overhead capitalised at about ten times. The interim filing discloses consolidated general and administrative expense of US$63.5m but no parent-only figure [S2], and we have not invented one. The direction of the omission is stated: it raises the parts and the target, the opposite of the conservative side. Its size is bounded rather than denied: the whole consolidated G&A is already an overstatement of the parent, and capitalising even that whole figure at ten times would exceed the parent's reported equity of US$347.2m, so it is an upper bound that cannot be used as a charge. We record the omission here and carry it in the signposts; it is a live source gap, not a silent zero [S2].

**The discount, and a mislabelled catalyst corrected.** The discount is the base rate, not the opportunity. House practice is that holding-company discounts persist indefinitely, and the question is not whether CUAN trades below its parts but whether a named, dated catalyst will close the gap. We hold the discount at the middle of the house band, 30%: there is no holdco-level buyback or tender, no asset sale or subsidiary listing, and no change in upstreaming policy [S0]. The Petrosea rights issue is a capital call on the group, not a distribution to it, and the last edition was wrong to call it a dated narrowing catalyst; a capital call dilutes rather than crystallises the mark [S9, S11]. The name's own five-year discount history cannot be computed (it listed recently; no entity-level sum-of-the-parts series exists in the data we hold), so the house base rate is the only anchor and we say so [S0]. We sit above the bottom of the band because the governance file argues for a wider discount, and short of the wide end because the sanction attaches to a listing participant rather than the company and the round's licence-freeze is another issuer's underwriter licence [S8]. The FY2026 audit at the end of April 2027 is the monitor we set [S2].

**Below-market sensitivity.** The base itself is the below-market mark the ruling requires: the 46.7% stake at US$321.4m of reported equity for the whole company, not at the US$2,182.1m market capitalisation. On that basis the SOTP returns Rp39 a share and the twelve-month fundamental value is Rp46; with the konglo lens the target is Rp323, and the regime scenarios span Rp86 to Rp734. A further impairment of Petrosea's book passes into the parts one for one with our 46.7% share of the write-down; the market mark, if it were ever used again, would add back the premium the group-consistency rule now excludes.

**The earnings cross-check is struck.** Last round the blend carried a P/E leg at a load-bearing weight; it capitalised the last audited year's parent profit, which is not earnings but a non-cash investment gain — the group's profit before tax of US$149.3m is smaller than its other operating income of US$193.7m, so on a normalised basis the group was loss-making on operations in its last audited year [S2]. Capitalising that at a peer multiple was unsupported optimism in a load-bearing number, and we have removed the leg rather than keep it at a token weight. The method set is therefore the primary plus a single cross-check. The P/BV method applies 0.9 to parent book and lands 21.8% versus the primary — ABOVE it, not below, because the SOTP carries the discount while the book cross-check does not [S0, S3]. The target is therefore set by the parts.

**What does the price imply?** Run the primary method backwards and today's price is not consistent with any discount inside the house band: the blended value before discount, carried forward at the cost of equity, is Rp40 a share, and even a zero holding-company discount leaves the parts far below the traded price [S0]. The engine reports no bracketing solution for the reverse discount, which is the finding: the market is not applying a discount to these parts, it is pricing something not in them [S0]. The plausible candidate is the platform story — a controlling shareholder, a listed contractor priced at many times its book, an acquisition pipeline with a named target still in negotiation, and a new-energy portfolio with no contracted cash flow [S2, S11, S7]. We can say the parts we can source do not support the price; we cannot say what does, and we do not invent it [S0].

**The konglo lens is the last step, and it is what makes the target.** The parts give a twelve-month fundamental value of Rp46 a share and a value today of Rp40; the price is Rp505, so the market pays 12.5 times the value today. An ordinary name would be carried at the fundamental value rolled forward; a konglo name is not, because the marginal price is set by a concentrated float, so the premium over the parts is a regime variable, not a fundamental one [S0]. The lens measures the price against the value and keeps part of the gap for the twelve-month horizon. For this name the regime flags are live and dated: the enforcement round that names CUAN [S8] and the index treatment of concentrated-ownership names [S13, S14]. The base regime case — the most likely path, 35% of the log gap closed in the year after the enforcement adjustment — lands at Rp236, and the probability-weighted result of the regime scenarios is the target of Rp323 [S0]. That is the most likely twelve-month price, not the base regime scenario itself; the regime bear is Rp86 and the regime bull Rp734, and their probability weight produces the target. No fundamental input is bent: the fundamental value is built from the parts alone and the lens is applied afterwards [S0].

The sensitivity grid runs the holding-company discount against the cost of equity, because those are now the two variables that move this valuation [S0]. It is compressed at the top: a narrower discount helps, but cannot bridge the gap to the traded price on its own, because the parts are the constraint — a holdco's target is set by what it holds.

**The mark is a book mark now, so the risk is impairment, not the tape.** The largest part is a stake in Petrosea carried at its share of PTRO's reported equity [S3]. The traded evidence that the equity is fragile is still worth stating: PTRO's market capitalisation is US$2,182.1m at the 15 October 2026 price on US$321.4m of equity and US$1.3m of continuing half-year profit; the shares fell sharply on the rights-issue news [S11, F53] and were volatile enough that the exchange wrote to the company, which replied that it had withheld no material fact and that it was aware of MSCI's evaluation of the Indonesian market [S10, F78]. That premium is excluded from the base, but a de-rating of the tape is still a signal about the durability of the book: if Petrosea's earnings and equity are marked down, the book mark falls with them, and the discount is the channel that carries the impairment into the target. The rights issue dilutes a holder that does not subscribe by up to 1.7%, is capped at 1.7% of Petrosea's capital, and leaves the parent a choice between laying out cash for its 46.7% share and accepting the dilution [S9]; the subscription price is not yet disclosed, so we size it as a claim on the group's US$220.2m of cash rather than a fixed number [S9, S3].

**The largest mark is partly self-supported.** This is the bear point the last edition missed. CUAN's own subsidiary, PT Kreasi Jasa Persada (KJP) — not an outside affiliate — bought more than IDR865.0bn of PTRO shares in March 2025 and a further IDR10.0bn tranche on 24 July 2025 [S12], lifting the group's stake from 41.9% to 45.3% during 2025 and to 46.7% at 30 June 2026 [S2, S3]. The parent has therefore used its own capital to support the price of the asset that dominates its parts. The base carries that asset at book rather than at the supported price, which limits the damage, but the governance read is a bear point in its own right: a de-rating of PTRO would be reinforced if the parent's buying stopped, and the buying is a use of the same cash the group needs for its debt service and its acquisition pipeline. We add it to the bear narrative and to the discount rationale, not to a footnote.

**The control basis is thin.** The group consolidates Petrosea on the strength of a control statement given by CRO, a shareholder holding 34.0%, on 7 November 2023, not on an outright majority [S3]. The group's 46.7% stake is the largest, and there is no history of the other shareholders forming a voting group, but a third-party letter is a weaker foundation than ownership, and a change in that shareholder's position would put the consolidation — and the SOTP's largest line — in question [S3].

**The discount can widen while you wait.** The house base rate is that these discounts persist and no catalyst to narrow this one is present; the group's dividend is a token (US$2.0m in FY2025), so there is no cash return while you wait [S2]. That carry risk is what makes a wide discount on its own an insufficient thesis.

**Governance and regulatory risk.** The regulator's enforcement round names CUAN alongside two other Barito-linked issuers, with a sanction falling on a subscriber over concealed orders in CUAN's own listing [S8]. The round's licence-freeze headline is an underwriter's licence in another issuer's case, and the further participant sanctions fall on exchange members, not on CUAN or its mining licences — we checked the scope and it touches no licence of this group [S8]. Related-party revenue was US$34.6m in the half year [S3]. Neither is a manipulation-class finding — both are disclosed — but both widen the warranted discount, which is why we sit above the bottom of the band [S8, S3].

**Financing and liquidity risk.** Net debt is large against an EBITDA the half year only just covers after interest, finance expense was US$57.5m in a single half year against gross profit of US$101.6m, and the model does not repay debt [S3, S0]. The capital programme has been funded with bank facilities and two phases of a shelf bond and sukuk programme, so any interruption to capital access is a direct risk to the ramp [S3, F56].

**Execution risk.** The SINI acquisition remains in negotiation with no agreed price or timetable [S2]; we exclude it from the base case, though the larger reserve figure the company projects depends on it.

The scenarios shock two inputs, mirrored in both directions: the holding-company discount, widened to the extremes the engine admits, and the cost of equity [S0]. The marks are static sourced book values the engine does not itself shock; since Petrosea is the largest part, the discount is the channel that reaches it, and we say so rather than imply a test we cannot run [S0]. The revenue-path shock the first edition carried is dropped, not kept: the parts are static marks, so a revenue shock moved no valuation input at all and bought false width. The spread the two live shocks produce is real rather than cosmetic, because it moves the marks through the discount. The bear case pushes the discount past the top of the house band, lifts the cost of equity, and reads as an impairment of the book as the absence of a narrowing catalyst bites and the parent's own buying stops; the bull is the parts being worth more than book: Petrosea publishes and is re-marked at a house value above equity, the SINI acquisition closes and adds reserves, and the discount narrows below the bottom of the band [S9, S2]. Even the bull leaves the parts short of the traded price: what would move the rating from above is a mark we can source (a published PTRO house value, a priced SINI deal, or a crystallised stake value), not a narrower discount. Signposts that would change the view are a holdco-level capital return; a priced SINI transaction; a stake increase or disposal that crystallises a mark; and the FY2026 audited accounts [S2, S3].

**The konglo lens carries its own regime scenarios, separate from the business cases above** [S0]. Where the business scenarios shock the discount and the cost of equity, the regime scenarios keep a different share of the premium over fundamental value, because for a konglo name that share is what the float and the flow calendar decide, not the business [S0]. On the lens's own probabilities the bear regime lands at Rp86, the base at Rp236 and the bull at Rp734: the bear gives most of the premium back as the float and the index flows turn against concentrated-ownership names, the bull keeps and even extends it, and the weighted base gives the target. The regime catalysts are dated and we watch them: the exchange's minimum-free-float rule, where the annual report's public holding of 15.9% leaves less than a percentage point of headroom to the fifteen-per-cent floor even though the snapshot figure of 18.6% looks comfortable, so a small sell-down requirement is live [S2, S0]; the index provider's review of Indonesia's treatment of concentrated-ownership names, deciding by 30 June 2027 [S14]; the enforcement file that names CUAN [S8]; and any group corporate action. A change of control would be the one event that resets the lens, and no offer is on the table [S2].

Control sits with Prajogo Pangestu's Barito interests. On the annual report's own register at the end of 2025 he holds 84.1% directly and the public holds 15.9% across tens of thousands of holders [S2]. The data pack's snapshot shows insider holdings of 82.2% and a free float of 18.6%, and the two registers do not sum alike; we use the annual report's register as the primary ownership figure and reconcile the snapshot to it rather than quoting one against the other [S2, S0]. Against the exchange's fifteen-per-cent floor the annual report's public figure leaves less than a percentage point of headroom, not the comfortable cushion the snapshot implies, so a forced float increase is a live possibility rather than a remote one [S2, S0, S1]. The company was assembled by acquisition, and its most valuable asset is a listed company it controls through its own shares and a third party's control statement, a structure that concentrates decision-making further [S3].

The konglo profile, in the group context. CUAN is the integrated mining arm of the Barito group, the conglomerate of Prajogo Pangestu, alongside the group's coal-price and renewables vehicles and the listed contractor it consolidates [S2, S11]. The controller and affiliates hold the great majority of the register — the annual report puts Prajogo at 84.1% — and the konglo table below draws on the exchange snapshot's 18.6% free float, which we flag as the snapshot figure and not the annual-report register (

) [S2, S0]. The group trades with itself: consolidated revenue from related parties was US$34.6m in the half year [S3]. And the parent has bought its own listed subsidiary on the market: KJP, CUAN's subsidiary, bought more than IDR865.0bn of PTRO shares in March 2025 and further tranches through the year [S12], lifting the group's stake from 41.9% to 45.3% and then to 46.7% [S2, S3]. That flow supports the mark and is why the mark is treated as partly self-supported in sections four and five, not as an arm's-length price. The regime backdrop is adverse and dated: concentrated-ownership names were removed from the global index provider's Standard index at its May 2026 review — CUAN among them — and the provider has opened a consultation on reclassifying Indonesia to Standalone Market status, with a decision by 30 June 2027 [S13, S14]. The regulator's enforcement round names CUAN [S8]. Pledged-share disclosure and auditor changes are not flagged in the material published this cycle; we record that as absence of evidence, not a clean bill [S2]. The dividend is a token (US$2.0m), so the group's cash needs, not a distribution policy, govern what reaches minority holders [S2].

The regulatory file is the most material governance item and it is dated. In October 2026 the capital markets regulator handed over administrative sanction letters from an enforcement round that includes CUAN alongside two other issuers in the same group, with a fine of IDR100.0bn on a subscriber that concealed its share-order information in CUAN's own public offering and a larger fine on a subscriber over another issuer's listing [S8]. The sanction attaches to a listing participant rather than the company, but it is a governance-discount input, not a footnote. The scope is precise: the round's licence-freeze is an underwriter's licence in the DSSA case and the further participant sanctions fall on exchange members and market participants — none on CUAN or its mining licences [S8]. It is the single most recent dated event in this name [S8].

Related-party dealings are a structural feature rather than an exception: consolidated revenue from related parties was US$34.6m in the half year, and the group's facilities have the parent as a joint borrower with the operating subsidiaries [S3]. The FVTPL portfolio of US$228.8m is also a related-party question we cannot close: the LK says it is invested in non-financial institutions but does not name the issuers, so we cannot confirm whether they sit in related or group institutions — that is absence of evidence, not a clean bill [S3]. Pledged-share disclosure and auditor changes are not flagged in the material the company has published in this cycle; we record that as an absence of evidence rather than a clean bill of health [S2]. On dividends the record is thin: a token distribution of US$2.0m, approved in April and paid in May 2025, with no interim policy since [S2]. On ESG the group discloses a mine reclamation and closure provision, and the larger exposure is the domestic-market obligation together with the permitting footprint of a rapidly acquired licence base [S2, S3].

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter: the regulator's sanction letters, already delivered [S8]; the listed subsidiary's general meeting on its rights issue, which we watch for the take-up and the price [S9]; the FY2027 work-plan approval, which sets the tonnage ceiling [S7]; the FY2026 audit [S2]; and the index provider's decision on Standalone status by 30 June 2027, the regime event that governs the concentrated-ownership complex [S14].

Between updates we monitor four things. The published PTRO mark and, when it comes, its coverage house value, because the stake is the largest part of the SOTP [S11, S3]. The group's mines' reported invested capital and licence status, because the coal mark is a carrying value that moves with the concession base and its depletion [S3, S7]. The half-year margin and the cash conversion, because the last audited year's profit was mostly non-cash [S3, S2]. And the financing and the parent's stake-buying: the debt maturity ladder, any new facility, and KJP's purchases, because the model does not repay debt, the finance charge consumes most of the operating margin, and the parent's buying is a use of the same cash [S3, S12].

base.narrative: The parts as they stand: the Petrosea stake at PTRO's reported book equity, the group's own mines at their reported invested capital, the exploration portfolio at its carrying value, the FVTPL portfolio at fair value, group cash-only net debt less the listed subsidiary's debt taken by entity, and a 30% holding-company discount with no narrowing catalyst yet dated.

bear.narrative: The book itself is impaired and the discount widens: the coal-price cycle and the thin margins force an impairment of the mining properties and of Petrosea's reported equity, so the stake and the concessions marked at book are worth less than book, and the FVTPL portfolio marks down in an adverse tape. The discount is the channel that carries an impairment into the target — it widens PAST the top of the 20-40% house band as the OJK file stays open and the 23 November rights issue is taken up only partially, diluting the stake without bringing cash to the holdco. The partly self-supported mark is a bear point in its own right: Kreasi Jasa Persada, CUAN's own subsidiary, has been the buyer of PTRO shares, so a de-rating would be reinforced if the parent's buying stopped. The higher cost of equity the balance-of-payments regime implies is charged on the whole, coal demand discipline keeps the group's own tonnage at the plan rather than above it, and the SINI acquisition does not close, so the projected reserve base stays at the 228.29 Mt already on the books.

bull.narrative: The parts are worth more than book: Petrosea publishes, is initiated, and its house value — or a sustained market value — is above its reported equity, so the parent's stake is re-marked up; the rights issue funds its engineering and construction book and the parent takes up its share to keep the 46.71% whole; the SINI acquisition closes and adds reserves to the concessions already marked; the group's 30 Mt/yr ambition and the coking-coal start are delivered. A holdco-level catalyst then crystallises the discount towards the narrow end of the band — a higher upstream dividend, a sub-level capital return or a stake sale at a mark — and the cost of equity falls as the balance-of-payments pressure eases.

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E set at 24%, below the half year's own pace: 1H2026 consolidated revenue of US$736.105m was up 59% on the comparable half of 2025 (S3), so a full year at that run rate would be far above the FY2025A base of US$1,215.618m; 24% is the taper towards the long-run coal-ramp pace as the group plan of >30 Mt/yr by 2031 (F13) and the >US$1bn order book are absorbed. No decline is assumed: costs and volumes follow the last actual.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Held at the 1H2026 LK margin: gross profit US$101.627m on revenue US$736.105m (S3) = 13.8%. The FY2023-25 average (22.0%) is distorted by the pre-acquisition FY2023 base and is not the current economics; the method card says costs stay at the last actual in real terms.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Stripped of the half-year's other operating income, which the red team correctly says we must not capitalise. 1H2026 gross profit US$101.627m less operating profit US$68.499m gives a cost block of US$33.128m on revenue US$736.105m, but that operating profit already carries other operating income of +US$9.060m (S3 note 40, part-quoted F68), so the ex-other-income cost is US$42.188m = 5.73% of revenue. The half-year's other income is not recurring: it is a US$42.717m FX gain (F69) net of a US$13.149m credit-loss allowance (F71) and a US$14.352m fair-value loss on the FVTPL portfolio (F70), the same non-cash mix the report condemns in FY2025A. This line also carries the final tax the LK charges above operating profit (US$4.847m, F72), which is why the forecast tax rate below is not the group's combined tax burden.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the 1H2026 LK depreciation, depletion and amortisation of US$93.619m on revenue US$736.105m (S3) = 12.7% — the FY2023-25 default (5.9%) understates a group whose mining properties and stripping assets are now US$381.867m (S3). This half-year figure is the full charge (all three elements), and it is the honest full-year rate. History is now keyed on the SAME basis: the FY2025A da fact (F82) is the full group charge of US$155.318m from the operating-segment note (S2), not the cost-of-revenue depreciation component alone, so the FY+1 forecast rate and the last actual year are measured on one footing.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the 1H2026 run rate: acquisitions of property, plant and equipment of US$72.901m on revenue US$736.105m (S3), i.e. 9.9% annualised. The FY2024-25 default (21.9%) is an acquisition-era number and is not a maintenance spend.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Reverted from the engine default to the last-actual balance sheet. The FY2023-25 average (34.09%) is an artefact of the pre-acquisition FY2023 base, when the group carried almost no working capital; the last balance sheet (30 June 2026, S0 latest_bs) carries working capital of US$278.437m against an annualised revenue base of US$1,472.210m, i.e. 18.91%. Holding that ratio is the most-likely reading: the coal ramp and the new offshore EPCI line both build receivables and contract assets, and no source shows the ratio falling.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Set from the LK's own arithmetic rather than asserted: the half-year income tax charge below profit before tax is US$5.443m (F73, note 25) on profit before tax of US$14.287m (S3) = 38.1%. The earlier 10% note was wrong — it was neither the statutory rate nor the effective one. The final tax regime is already a cost in the opex line above (US$4.847m in the half year, F72, charged above operating profit), so this rate is the below-the-line charge only and the two do not double-count. The rate is high because the half-year pre-tax base is thin: operating profit of US$68.499m carries US$57.513m of finance expense.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Blended coupon on the reported debt: 1H2026 finance expenses of US$57.513m annualised on opening debt of US$1,448.749m (S3) implies ~8%, and the group's public bonds and sukuk carry 6.75-9.00% coupons (S3); set at 8.5%.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Held at the 1H2026 run rate: finance income of US$3.301m annualised over opening cash of US$453.801m (S3) = ~1.5%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: the group funded itself in 1H2026 with net new bank loans of US$59.6m but repaid as much as it drew (S3), and no sourced refinancing plan exists at the parent beyond the Petrosea rights issue, which is at the subsidiary.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Set to the non-controlling interests' share of group equity at 30 June 2026, 291.210 / (347.161 + 291.210) = 45.62% (F67 and F54, S3), because the profit-attribution routes do not produce a forward rate. The 1H2026 attribution is parent US$19.780m against non-controlling interests of MINUS US$3.316m (F58, F59, S3 p.8) — a negative minority share driven by the US$7.620m discontinued profit (F57) that accrues to Petrosea's 53.29% minority (F66) and by loss-making continuing operations at Equator Sumber Energi; capitalising either number would flatter parent earnings in a way no source supports. The FY2023-25 average (4.81%) cannot represent the forward group either: it is dominated by the pre-acquisition FY2023 base, when the group was one small coal miner, while 53.29% of Petrosea and 35.00% of Equator Sumber Energi now sit outside the parent. The equity proportion is the reproducible structural anchor.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Held at ~2% of parent earnings: the FY2025 AGMS approved a cash dividend of US$2.000m, or US$0.00017791 a share (S2/F29-F30), which is ~1.5% of FY2025 parent profit; the group is a capital-hungry acquisition vehicle, not a dividend payer.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: 112,418,900,000 shares after the 1:10 stock split (S2/F31); the Petrosea rights issue is at the subsidiary, not the parent (S9/S11), and such parent-level issue as it implies (a maximum 1.66% dilution of the listed stake, F75) is carried as a risk, not as a parent share change.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for the reporting currency: the group reports in US dollars (S3) so the dollar cap of 2.5% applies and the long-run rate is held at the 2.0% house default rather than at the group's own growth, which is an acquisition artefact and not a terminal rate.

assumptions.label: Holding-company discount to SOTP
assumptions.basis: Held at 30%, the middle of the 20-40% house band, and the choice is argued rather than asserted. The name's own five-year discount history cannot be computed — the group listed in 2023 and no entity-level SOTP series exists in the data we hold (S0 own_history is empty) — so the house base rate for holdcos, that 20-40% persists indefinitely by default, is the only anchor available; we say so rather than implying an own-history check we could not run. We widen from the bottom of the band to 30% for the governance file: the OJK enforcement round names CUAN alongside DSSA and BREN, with a Rp100bn fine on a subscriber that concealed its order book in CUAN's own listing (S8/F36), and the further participant sanctions in the same round attach to the CUAN case (F77). We do not go to the wide end for a stated reason: the sanction is on a listing participant, not on the company, the licence-freeze in the round is an underwriter's licence in the DSSA case and touches no mining licence of this group (F76), and the PTRO stake is now carried at its reported book equity rather than at the market's premium, which is already the conservative mark, so a top-of-band discount would double-count caution. A dated narrowing catalyst exists and is tracked: Petrosea's RUPSLB on 23 November 2026 for the rights issue (S9, S11) — a capital call on the group, not a distribution to it, which is why the discount is not narrowed now (and it is not a narrowing catalyst: §4 says so plainly). The scenario tails deliberately run past the band (bear 45%, bull 15%): the discount is the only channel the scenario layer has into a static mark, so the tails test whether a further impairment can move the target, and a symmetric +/-0.15 is the widest shock the engine admits (S0).

challenges.challenge: VAL_KONGLO_REGIME §4 is explicit: a covered listed subsidiary is marked at house value, and a sibling that is itself a konglo name and not yet covered must not be marked at market — the parent waits in draft. PTRO is konglo:true (cov_konglo show) and uncovered (coverage/companies/PTRO.JK holds only fund record; queue 'initiation:PTRO.JK:2026-10-27' is status queued, version 0). Yet the SOTP marks CUAN's 46.71% at PTRO's 15 Oct 2026 market capitalisation of US$2,182.1m (F38), US$1,019.3m and 70.5% of the US$1,445.5m gross parts. That imports PTRO's own konglo premium into CUAN's fundamental value (Rp91), which the lens then multiplies, so the SELL target of Rp357 is overstated by whatever PTRO's premium is. Disclosure of the market mark does not cure a method breach; BRPT.JK was held in draft for the identical uncovered-konglo-sibling issue.
challenges.answer: Accepted; the Director ruled on 2026-10-28 that the stage machine cannot return the ticker to draft, so the SOTP carries the 46.71% PTRO stake at PTRO's reported total equity (F48, US$321.393m) times the stake, labelled method book. The market capitalisation (F38, US$2,182.1m at 15 Oct 2026) is disclosed but excluded from the fundamental and the target; §4 states plainly that PTRO is uncovered, that the listed premium is excluded by the group-consistency rule and that the mark switches to house value once PTRO publishes. The below-market book mark is the base and the resulting fundamental and target are published in §4 (the sensitivity paragraph). No PTRO premium enters the target.

challenges.challenge: The SOTP deducts holdco net debt of US$652.035m, computed as group debt US$1,426.519m less cash US$220.245m (F61) less 'other financial assets' US$228.847m (F62) less Petrosea debt US$325.392m. Note 6 [S3 p.97] says the US$228.847m is 'investasi pada institusi non-keuangan ... diukur pada FVTPL' - investments in non-financial institutions, not cash or deposits. §4 never states the US$652.0m or that US$228.8m of non-cash investments are netted against debt. On the engine's own arithmetic the treatment is worth about US$160.2m after the 30% discount, roughly Rp26/share or 30% of the Rp86.8 SOTP, and it is the value-generous direction for a SELL.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Note six of the interim LK says the US$228.847m (F62) is investments in non-financial institutions measured at FVTPL at quoted bid prices in an active market — equity securities, not demand deposits. The portfolio is now carried as a separate SOTP asset at fair value and is no longer netted against debt; holdco net debt is cash-only (cash F61 only). §4 states the arithmetic component by component, identifies the portfolio and explains the change; §6 records that the LK does not name the issuers, so related-party status cannot be confirmed and is recorded as absence of evidence.

challenges.challenge: §6 says 'affiliates of the controller have bought the listed subsidiary's shares on the market' [S3, S12]. S12 says the buyer is PT Kreasi Jasa Persada (KJP), CUAN's own subsidiary: 2.6m PTRO shares at an average Rp3,847 on 24 July 2025 after a March 2025 programme worth more than Rp865bn. S2 p.10 records KJP moving from 41.91% to 45.33% in 2025, and S3 puts the stake at 46.71% at 30 June 2026. The parent has therefore used its own capital to support the price of the asset that is 70% of its SOTP, and the reader meets this only as a neutral 'related-party flow that supports the mark', never as a bear point or a reason to discount the mark.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The buyer is named as CUAN's own subsidiary PT Kreasi Jasa Persada, and sized from the record: more than Rp865bn of PTRO shares in March 2025 (F96) and a further ~Rp10bn on 24 July 2025 (F97), lifting the stake from 41.91% (F98) to 45.33% (F99) in 2025 and to 46.71% (F39) at 30 June 2026. §4 and §5 now state that the largest mark is partly self-supported, that a de-rating would be reinforced if the parent's buying stopped, and carry it in the bear narrative and the discount rationale rather than as a neutral related-party flow.

challenges.challenge: The MSCI regime facts are cited to [S10], but the archived S10 (emitennews, 4,472 chars) contains no '2027', no 'Standalone' and no May 2026 deletion; it only reports that PTRO is aware of 'evaluasi MSCI terhadap pasar modal Indonesia'. challenges.answer: Accepted. The S10 citation was wrong and is removed from the MSCI facts. We archived two registered sources into the company record: S13 (investortrust, 13 May 2026) for the May 2026 Standard Index deletion that includes CUAN, and S14 (MSCI's own consultation release, 15 Oct 2026) for the Standalone proposal and the decision on or before 30 June 2027. §4, §5, §6 and the frontmatter catalyst now cite [S13] and [S14], each dated.

challenges.challenge: §1 and §6 state '82.2% of the register is insider-held' and a 'free float of 18.6%' [S2, S0]. S2 (Annual Report 2025, p.115) shows Prajogo Pangestu at 84.076% and the public at 15.924% (17,901,250,000 of 112,418,900,000 shares) at 31 Dec 2025. Neither quoted figure is the AR's: 18.58% is the IDX snapshot and 82.2% is Yahoo, and the two sum to 100.8%. Against the 15% floor the AR's public figure leaves about 0.9pp of headroom, not the ~3.6pp the report implies when it says 'no forced float increase is due'.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The annual report's register is now the primary ownership figure: Prajogo 84.076% (F94) and public 15.924% (F95) at 31 December 2025. §1 and §6 reconcile the Yahoo/IDX snapshot (82.2%/18.6%) to the register rather than quoting one against the other, restate the headroom to the fifteen-per-cent floor as less than a percentage point, and state that the konglo table draws on the exchange snapshot (18.58%), not the register.

challenges.challenge: §4 says 'the subsidiary's borrowings sit inside the consolidated debt we deduct [S3]', but the SOTP deliberately excludes Petrosea's US$325.392m debt because the stake is marked at market (an equity value already net of that debt) - see valuation.holdco_net_debt_note. The sentence says the opposite of the bridge and would lead a reader to double-count the debt or misread the holdco charge. The card's required look-through leverage is also absent.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The offending sentence is corrected: the SOTP deliberately excludes Petrosea's debt by entity and marks the stake at equity, so the subsidiary's borrowings are not inside the deducted charge. §4 now states the look-through figures and keeps the two debt stocks separate: the holdco charge (cash-only, after removing Petrosea's named debt legs F51/F88/F89/F92/F93) plus the group's 46.71% share of Petrosea's debt, measured against clean FY2025A EBITDA of EBIT plus the full D&A (F82).

challenges.challenge: VAL_HOLDCO_DISCOUNT §1 requires holdco opex capitalised at about 10x, deducted from the SOTP. The model carries none; the only mention is the orphan justification valuation.holdco_opex, which says the parent-only figure is undisclosed so no charge is made. §4 is silent, and the omission raises the value and the SELL target - the opposite of the 'conservative direction' the report claims for the unattributed bank lines. An upper bound is available (consolidated G&A US$63.510m, F22) even if it overstates the parent.
challenges.answer: Accepted. No parent-only cost line is published, so no charge is invented. §4 now states the omission, its direction (it raises the parts and the target) and its size: consolidated G&A of F22 is an overstatement of the parent, and capitalising even that whole figure at ten times would exceed parent equity of F54, so it is an unusable upper bound. The orphan justification valuation.holdco_opex is deleted and the reasoning moves into §4.
